title: The Silk Road: More Than a Trade Route
text:
For more than 1,500 years, a network of routes known as the Silk Road connected China with the Mediterranean. Although silk was one of the most valuable goods transported along it, merchants also carried spices, paper, glass, horses and precious metals. Cities such as Kashgar, Samarkand and Bukhara grew rich because they were located at important crossroads.

However, the Silk Road was not only about trade. Ideas, religions and technologies travelled along the same paths. Buddhism spread from India to China, while papermaking and, later, gunpowder made their way westwards. Musicians, scholars and craftsmen exchanged knowledge in the busy markets and caravanserais, where travellers could rest and their animals could be fed.

The journey itself was extremely dangerous. Caravans had to cross the Taklamakan Desert, whose name is often said to mean "you go in, but you never come out". Few merchants travelled the entire distance; instead, goods passed from hand to hand, and prices rose with every stage. Today, historians regard the Silk Road as one of the earliest examples of globalisation.
